name: Payne's Grey
poem: A deep blue-grey invented by an 18th-century English watercolourist — never quite black, never quite blue, perfect for the gloom of an English sky.

recipe.note: A deep blue-grey — blue and black, never truly neutral.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Named for William Payne, an obscure 18th-century English watercolourist whose grey became, against the odds, one of the most widely-used colours of the 20th century.

entries.title: Topographical Watercolours
entries.blurb: Payne taught watercolour in Exeter and Plymouth, and used his self-mixed grey for atmospheric shadows in landscape washes. The colour outlasted his reputation by two centuries.

entries.title: Turner's Storm Studies
entries.meta: J. M. W. Turner · early 19th c.
entries.blurb: Turner used a grey almost identical to Payne's for the underwash of his Channel sea-pieces — a colour with enough blue to suggest sky reflected in dark water.

entries.title: Architectural Renderings
entries.blurb: Payne's grey became the standard wash for architectural drawings — its slight blueness made shadows look cool and stone look cold, on every Victorian elevation.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: A grey with enough blue in it to feel intentional — the colour of menswear that doesn't want to be quite as serious as charcoal.

entries.title: Victorian Half-Mourning
entries.blurb: After a year of pure black, Victorian widows transitioned through grey and mauve before returning to colour — Payne's grey was the standard "second-stage" wash for ribbons and trim.

entries.title: The Modern Business Suit
entries.blurb: The contemporary blue-grey suit — softer than charcoal, more formal than dove — is Payne's grey applied to wool. The colour suggests authority without aggression.

entries.title: Industrial Chic
entries.blurb: The reclaimed-steel colour palette that defined post-industrial interior design — exposed beams, cement floors, kitchen pendants — settled on Payne's grey as its baseline.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Payne's grey is the colour of weather — not weather happening, but weather about to happen.

entries.title: Storm Clouds
entries.blurb: The underbelly of a storm cloud, lit from below by reflected ground light — exactly Payne's grey, with the same hidden warmth as the pigment's tiny white component.

entries.title: Slate
entries.blurb: Roofing slate from Welsh quarries weathers to the precise Payne's grey of every English village — a colour the pigment was probably trying to reproduce.

entries.title: Wet Stone Walls
entries.blurb: The dry-stone walls of the English uplands, soaked by rain, deepen to Payne's grey — the exact colour William Payne mixed to render them in his teaching books.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Payne's grey has quietly become the default colour of professional rendering — it shows up wherever someone wants depth without commitment.

entries.title: Architectural Visualisation
entries.blurb: Architectural visualisation defaults to Payne's grey for the sky in unbuilt buildings — the colour reads as both cloudy and aspirational, never weather-specific.

entries.title: Sketch Artist's Standard
entries.blurb: Courtroom and forensic sketch artists keep Payne's grey on their palette as a one-colour solution — eyes, hair, jacket all rendered in dilutions of the same wash.

entries.title: Cinematography Grading
entries.blurb: The blue-grey "teal and orange" look that dominated 2010s blockbusters owes its teal half to a digital cousin of Payne's grey — a colour producers find calming.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Almost uniquely among pigments, Payne's grey is named for a person — and the person was barely famous in his own lifetime.

entries.title: William Payne
entries.blurb: A drawing master in Exeter and Plymouth who taught aristocratic students. His teaching books were popular; his paintings were not. Only the grey survived.

entries.title: The Original Recipe
entries.blurb: Payne's published recipe was Prussian blue + crimson lake + yellow ochre — a mix you can still get from any decent watercolour set. The brand-name grey came later.

entries.title: The Brand Name
entries.blurb: The London colourmen Winsor & Newton industrialised Payne's recipe in tube form — and "Payne's Grey" became a commercial pigment name that has outlived its referent.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Payne's grey carries one of the more precise emotional ranges of any colour — melancholy without despair, restraint without coldness.

entries.title: Melancholy
entries.blurb: The colour of the Romantic Sublime — Wordsworth's clouds, Friedrich's seascapes. A grey deep enough to mean weather but blue enough to mean longing.

entries.title: Industrial Age
entries.blurb: After the Industrial Revolution, Payne's grey acquired a second meaning — the colour of smog, soot-stained brick, riveted steel. Romance turned to atmosphere.

entries.title: Transition
entries.blurb: In contemporary colour theory, Payne's grey is taught as the model "chromatic neutral" — never just grey, always grey-and-something, the colour of conditional choices.
